polar-bear.anatomy: Polar bears have longer necks and narrower heads than other bears, a streamlined shape that helps when swimming and when reaching into seal holes. Their fur has two layers: a dense underfur and long, transparent guard hairs with hollow cores that scatter light, making the bear look white or cream. Underneath, black skin absorbs heat, and a fat layer up to 10 centimetres thick provides insulation and buoyancy. Their huge front paws, up to 30 centimetres across, work as paddles in the water and spread their weight on thin ice; the soles are partly furred and covered with small bumps for grip. Their claws are short, thick and curved for gripping ice and seizing prey. Polar bears have a superb sense of smell and can locate seals under snow, but they overheat easily when running, so they usually move slowly and save energy.
polar-bear.family: Polar bears mate on the sea ice in spring. The fertilised egg doesn't implant until autumn, and only if the female has built up enough fat. She then digs a maternity den in a snowdrift, often on land, and gives birth in midwinter, usually to twins. Cubs are born blind, with fine fur, weighing only around 600 grams. The family stays in the den for three to four months while the mother, who has not eaten since autumn, nurses them on milk that is very rich in fat. In March or April they emerge, and the cubs follow their mother onto the sea ice, where she teaches them to hunt. Cubs stay with her for about two and a half years. Males play no part in raising cubs, and sometimes kill them.
polar-bear.people: Inuit have lived alongside polar bears for thousands of years. The bear, called nanuq, holds an important place in their culture and stories, and Inuit hunters still harvest a limited number under co-management agreements, using the meat and hides. In 1973, the five countries with polar bears signed an agreement to protect them and their habitat, one of the first international wildlife treaties. Tourism has become important in Churchill, Manitoba, where visitors watch bears from tundra vehicles each autumn as they wait for Hudson Bay to freeze. The town runs a polar bear alert program and even has a 'polar bear jail' where problem bears are held until the ice forms, then released. Scientists use collars, aerial surveys and even genetic sampling of footprints in the snow to monitor populations.

narwhal.anatomy: Narwhals are medium-sized toothed whales with a rounded head, small mouth and short flippers that curl up at the tips in older animals. Young narwhals are blue-grey; adults are mottled grey and white, and older ones become almost white. They have no dorsal fin, only a low ridge along the back. Their famous tusk, usually found in males, grows from the left upper jaw and can reach about 3 metres. It spirals counterclockwise and is flexible, able to bend up to around 30 centimetres without breaking. Its surface has many tiny channels leading to nerves inside, which has led scientists to suggest it may sense changes in the water. Narwhals have a thick layer of blubber and can slow their heart rate dramatically on deep dives. Like other toothed whales, they use clicks, whistles and buzzes to echolocate and communicate.
narwhal.family: Narwhals live in groups called pods, often of 10 to 20, though thousands may gather during summer migrations. Males sometimes rub or cross tusks, a behaviour called tusking that may help them size each other up. Mating happens in spring, offshore in the pack ice. After a pregnancy of about 14 to 15 months, the female gives birth to a single calf, usually tail first, in summer. The calf is around 1.5 metres long and depends on its mother's rich milk for about 20 months, staying close to her side as the pod travels. Females give birth roughly every three years. Narwhals mature slowly, at around 6 to 9 years, and can live for 50 years or more. Orcas, polar bears and being trapped in freezing sea ice are their main natural threats.
narwhal.people: Inuit have hunted narwhals for centuries for their skin and blubber, called muktuk, which is rich in vitamin C and an important traditional food, as well as for their tusks. Medieval European traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, believed to cure poison; the Throne Chair of Denmark, made in the 1600s, is decorated with them. Today narwhal hunting is managed with quotas in Canada and Greenland, often set by Inuit organisations and governments together. Scientists work with Inuit hunters, who know narwhal behaviour intimately, to tag the whales and study their migrations. As sea ice shrinks, more shipping, mining and seismic surveys reach the Arctic; their noise can disturb narwhals, so some communities have pushed for protected areas, such as Tallurutiup Imanga national marine conservation area in Nunavut.

blue-whale.anatomy: A blue whale is long, slender and blue-grey, mottled with lighter patches. Under water it often looks bright blue. Its head is broad, flat and U-shaped from above, taking up nearly a quarter of its length. Instead of teeth, it has hundreds of baleen plates, made of keratin, hanging from its upper jaw, fringed with bristles that act as a sieve. Up to about 90 grooves run from its throat to its belly; when it feeds, these pleats expand like an accordion so it can engulf a huge mouthful of water and krill. Its blowhole spray rises up to 9 metres high. It has a small dorsal fin set far back on its body. Despite its size, a blue whale can reach speeds of around 30 km/h in short bursts and normally cruises much slower.
blue-whale.family: Blue whales are usually seen alone or in pairs, though they may gather where krill is plentiful. Little is known about their courtship. After a pregnancy of about 11 to 12 months, a female gives birth every two to three years, usually in warmer waters in winter. A newborn calf is around 7 metres long and weighs about 2.5 tonnes. It drinks very rich, fatty milk and gains weight extremely fast, until it is weaned at around six to seven months, by which time it may be about 16 metres long. Mothers and calves often travel together during this time. Blue whales reach maturity at around 5 to 15 years. Calves are vulnerable to orca attacks, but adults have almost no natural predators.
blue-whale.people: Blue whales were too fast and powerful for early whalers, but the invention of the explosive harpoon and steam-powered whaling ships in the late 1800s made them targets. During the 20th century, especially in the Antarctic, whalers killed hundreds of thousands, and by the 1960s they were near extinction. The International Whaling Commission protected them worldwide in 1966. Since then, some populations, such as those off California, have recovered substantially, while Antarctic blue whales remain a small fraction of their former numbers. Today, scientists use hydrophones to listen for their calls, satellite tags to follow them, and drones to measure their size and health. Whale watching has become a valuable industry. Ships slowing down in key areas, as many do off California, and proposals to move shipping lanes off Sri Lanka aim to reduce deadly collisions with these giants.

common-octopus.anatomy: An octopus has a soft, rounded body called the mantle, a head with two large eyes, and eight muscular arms lined with suckers. Each sucker can grip, taste and smell, and can move independently. The octopus has no bones; its only hard part is a parrot-like beak at the centre of its arms, so it can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak. It breathes with gills inside the mantle and moves by crawling or by jet propulsion, shooting water out of a tube called the siphon. Its skin contains thousands of colour-changing cells called chromatophores, plus reflective cells and muscles that raise bumps and spikes, letting it change both colour and texture in an instant. Its eyes are sharp but probably cannot see colour as we do. It has a large brain for an invertebrate, wrapped around its oesophagus.
common-octopus.family: Common octopuses live alone and are often cannibalistic, so mating can be risky. The male uses a specially modified arm, called the hectocotylus, to pass packets of sperm to the female, sometimes at arm's length. The female then finds a safe den and lays tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tiny eggs, hanging them in long strings from the roof. For weeks, sometimes months, depending on water temperature, she guards them without eating, blowing water over them to keep them clean and oxygenated and fending off predators. She dies soon after they hatch, and the male usually dies not long after mating. The hatchlings drift in the plankton for weeks, feeding on tiny animals, before settling on the seafloor. Very few survive.
common-octopus.people: Octopuses have been part of human cultures for thousands of years. Ancient Minoans painted them on pottery, and they appear in Japanese art, Greek cuisine and countless sea legends. Mediterranean fishers have long caught them in clay pots that octopuses use as dens. Scientists have been amazed by their intelligence: octopuses in aquariums have unscrewed jar lids, recognised individual keepers, squirted water at people they disliked, and escaped from tanks. Researchers study their arms for ideas in soft robotics. In 2021, a UK government review found strong evidence that octopuses can feel pain and are sentient, and they were included in British animal welfare law. Proposals to farm octopuses for food have drawn criticism from scientists and animal welfare groups.

leatherback-sea-turtle.anatomy: The leatherback is the only sea turtle without a hard shell. Its back is covered by leathery, oily skin over a mosaic of thousands of small bones, shaped into seven long ridges that run from head to tail and help it glide through water. It is usually dark grey or black, speckled with white, and has a pink spot on the top of its head that may be linked to sensing light and the seasons. Its front flippers are huge, spanning up to about 2.7 metres, and drive it across oceans. Its mouth has sharp, tooth-like points on its upper jaw, and its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that let water out while keeping jellyfish in. Its body can stay much warmer than cold water thanks to its size, fat insulation and a heat-exchange system in its flippers.
leatherback-sea-turtle.family: Leatherbacks mate at sea, and females return to tropical beaches every two to three years to nest, often to the same region where they hatched. On a nesting night, a female crawls up the beach, digs a deep hole with her hind flippers, and lays around 80 fertile eggs about the size of billiard balls, plus a layer of smaller, yolkless eggs whose purpose is still debated. She covers them and returns to the sea, and may nest several times in a season, about ten days apart. The eggs incubate in the warm sand for about two months; as with other turtles, warmer sand produces more females. The hatchlings dig out together, usually at night, and race to the water, guided by the brighter horizon over the sea. Very few survive to adulthood.
leatherback-sea-turtle.people: Leatherback eggs have been collected for food in many places, and in some countries this is now illegal or strictly managed. Since the 1960s, conservation programs have protected nesting beaches in places such as Trinidad, Costa Rica, French Guiana and Gabon, often run by local communities who patrol beaches at night, guard nests and lead turtle-watching tours. At sea, leatherbacks are often caught accidentally in fishing gear, so scientists have worked with fishers to develop changes like circle hooks and to close areas at key times. In Atlantic Canada, researchers have tagged leatherbacks feeding on jellyfish off Nova Scotia and found that some travel to nest in the Caribbean and South America. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches dark during nesting season and picking up plastic.

whale-shark.anatomy: The whale shark has a broad, flat head and a huge mouth at the very front of its snout, rather than underneath as in most sharks. Its dark grey to brownish body is covered with a pattern of pale spots and stripes, unique to each individual. Three prominent ridges run along each side of its back. Its skin can be up to 10 centimetres thick, making it one of the thickest skins of any animal. It has five large gill slits on each side, and inside its mouth are filter pads that sieve tiny food from the water. It also has thousands of tiny teeth, which it does not use for feeding. Scientists recently found that its eyes are protected by tiny tooth-like scales called denticles and that it can pull its eyeballs back into its head.
whale-shark.family: Very little is known about how whale sharks reproduce, as mating and birth have almost never been observed. In 1995, a pregnant female caught off Taiwan was found to be carrying about 300 developing young, at different stages, revealing that whale sharks hatch from eggs inside the mother and are born alive. Pups are born around 40 to 60 centimetres long. Scientists believe whale sharks mature slowly; males may not mature until they are around 25 to 30 years old and 8 to 9 metres long. Young whale sharks are rarely seen, and it is still not known where most are born. Many of the gatherings at feeding sites, such as Ningaloo or the Maldives, are dominated by young males.
whale-shark.people: In some places whale sharks were once hunted for their meat, fins and oil, but many countries now protect them, and international trade is regulated under CITES, the treaty that governs the global wildlife trade. In Vietnam, fishers call the whale shark 'Ca Ong', Mr Fish, and treat it with respect. Today, whale shark tourism supports local communities from Mexico and Belize to the Philippines and Western Australia; swimming alongside one is considered a bucket-list experience, and in places like Ningaloo strict guidelines limit how close swimmers get. Citizen science plays a large role in research: divers and tourists upload photos of the spots behind a shark's gills to global databases, where pattern-matching software originally developed for astronomers identifies individuals. These photo records have helped track thousands of whale sharks over years and across oceans.

strawberry-poison-frog.anatomy: The strawberry poison frog is tiny, around the size of a thumbnail. In many populations it is bright red with blue or black legs, but in the islands of Bocas del Toro, Panama, it comes in more than 15 colour forms: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and spotted. Bright colours warn predators of the alkaloid toxins in glands in its skin. Strongly coloured populations tend to be more toxic and bolder, while duller ones are more secretive. The frog has small pads on its toes for climbing among leaves. It is active by day and has good colour vision, which matters because frogs use colour to recognise mates of their own population. Its toxins are not produced by the frog but taken from mites and ants it eats and stored in its skin.
strawberry-poison-frog.family: Male strawberry poison frogs defend small territories on the forest floor, calling with a buzzing chirp. After mating, the female lays a handful of eggs, often three to five, in a moist spot on a leaf. The male guards them and keeps them moist, sometimes by carrying water. When the tadpoles hatch, the mother returns and carries each one on her back up into the trees, placing it alone in a small pool of water held in a bromeliad or other plant. Over the next weeks she visits each tadpole every few days and lays unfertilised eggs into the pool for it to eat. These eggs may pass on some of her toxins. After about six to eight weeks, the tadpole turns into a tiny frog and climbs out.
strawberry-poison-frog.people: Strawberry poison frogs belong to the family of poison dart frogs. Some members of that family, a few species from Colombia, have toxins strong enough that the Emberá, an Indigenous people of Colombia and Panama, used them on blowgun darts, giving the family its name, though the strawberry poison frog itself was not used this way. Because of their colours, these frogs are popular in the pet trade, and wild collection has threatened some island populations; today many are bred in captivity. Scientists study the Bocas del Toro populations to understand how new colours and species evolve, how toxins are gathered from food, and how frog parents care for their young. Compounds from poison frogs have inspired research into new painkillers. Tourists can see them in reserves such as Red Frog Beach in Bocas del Toro, which is named after them.
